Abstract
Human intelligence does not develop linearly: it follows a precise phase sequence. This article presents the hypothesis that this neurodevelopmental timeline corresponds to the dual-architecture artificial general intelligence (AGI) system previously proposed by the author, covering the 10 architectural components. We hypothesize that AGI development may be constrained by similar phase sequencing, address key objections (see
Sections 3.1
,
5.4
,
5.5
, and
5.6
for explicit objection-response pairs) through formal arguments, and provide indirect supporting evidence for six individual mechanisms on the MuJoCo platform: four-method anti-forgetting comparison: elastic weight consolidation (EWC), synaptic intelligence (SI), memory-aware synapses (MAS), and Naive. Curiosity-driven exploration, training stability analysis, multimodal cross-prediction, and warm-start routing analysis reveal negative transfer in genuinely novel scenarios, and a multi-novelty gradient experiment spanning five gravity levels (1.0×–2.0×) identifies a crossover threshold at approximately 1.25×–1.50× gravity on HalfCheetah-v5. An appendix provides a formal mathematical theory of token migration with two formal sketches and one implication.
1 Introduction: why AGI needs developmental biology
The dominant artificial intelligence (AI) paradigm assumes intelligence can be achieved through “larger models + more data.” However, the only known success case produced by 3.5 billion years of evolution, human intelligence, does not operate this way.
Humans are not born thinking. A newborn brain contains approximately 100 billion neurons, but cortical synaptic connections are sparse; executive function is near zero; there is no episodic memory, no language.
